author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: Steven Comes Home for Dinner
subtitle: The Lanternweald — expansion pass two
content:
Steven arrived with a casserole dish, a travel bag, and a question he had apparently been saving for three weeks.

"Does Dad really have a concert hall in another dimension now?"

Greg looked at the dish.

"Hey, buddy."

"Hi, Dad."

They hugged in the doorway of the car wash office, Greg's guitar case pressing awkwardly between them. Steven had grown into the kind of adult who could carry his own worries without announcing them, but the expression on his face was still bright when he saw his father.

I stood beside the kitchenette, trying not to feel like a furniture arrangement that had been added since his last visit.

Steven turned toward me.

"Jasper, right?"

"That's me."

"Dad's told me about you."

"All good things, I hope."

"Mostly. There was a very long story about a chair."

I covered my face.

Greg looked proud.

Dinner was supposed to happen at the little house near the beach. We'd bought vegetables and bread that morning. Greg had promised to cook; I had agreed to supervise because he had once described a microwave timer as a flexible suggestion.

Steven brought the casserole because he knew us both well enough to anticipate disaster.

It smelled of roasted squash and herbs. I set it on the counter and felt grateful for a practical offering that didn't require a speech.

We sat around the table as evening settled over Beach City. Through the open window came the sound of a car passing the boardwalk, followed by a gull with an opinion.

Steven asked about the Lanternweald.

Greg told him about Starwake Pier, the repaired railings, and the fundraiser. I told him about the seven neighborhoods and the fact that the magical doors did not turn the residents into fictional versions of themselves.

"So you can visit a place and still come back?" Steven asked.

"Yes," I said. "The doors are invitations. Not obligations."

He nodded slowly.

"Sounds nice."

Then he looked at Greg.

"Does it ever get confusing?"

Greg rested his fork on his plate.

"Which part?"

Steven glanced toward me, then back to his father.

"People coming and going. Knowing where home is. You used to worry about that stuff a lot."

For once Greg did not fill the silence with a joke.

"Yeah," he said. "I did. Still do, sometimes."

Steven waited.

I wanted to rescue the moment. I could have explained our relationship structure, described the agreements we'd made, and presented the whole thing as a reassuring story in which nobody ever felt jealous or uncertain.

That wouldn't have been fair to either of them.

Greg took a breath.

"Jasper and I have talked about what we want. They're ethically non-monogamous. They prefer polyamory, and we've agreed to be honest about our own boundaries instead of making promises neither of us means."

Steven looked at me.

"That works for you?"

"It's the kind of relationship I choose," I said. "But nobody else has to want it just because I do."

He nodded.

"And Dad?"

Greg smiled a little.

"I'm still learning. It's different from some things I've known. But Jasper's honest with me, and I get to say when I'm scared. That's a big deal."

Steven looked down at his plate.

"I'm glad you have that."

I saw Greg's shoulders loosen.

Then Steven added, "I'm not asking because I need to approve anything. I just want to know you're both okay."

"We're okay," Greg said.

I glanced at him.

"Most days."

He grinned.

"Hey."

"Some days we disagree about chairs."

Steven laughed.

The conversation shifted to the repaired pier. Steven wanted to see it. Greg offered to take him after dinner, but Steven looked exhausted from the journey.

"Maybe tomorrow," he said.

"Tomorrow's fine."

I took the plates to the sink while Greg and Steven talked about music. Greg had written a new song that left room in the melody. Steven wanted to hear it when he wasn't eating.

A little later I found Steven outside on the steps.

The night smelled of salt and cut grass. Lights shone along the boardwalk. He was sitting with his elbows on his knees, looking toward the water.

"Mind if I sit?" I asked.

"Sure."

I sat beside him.

For a while we watched a couple walk past with a dog that had a much better sense of where it wanted to go than its owners did.

"Do you think Dad feels like he's starting over?" Steven asked.

"Sometimes."

He looked at me.

"He spent so long being the person who waited for everyone else."

"I know."

"I don't want him to be lonely."

"Neither do I."

Steven rubbed his hands together.

"I've had to learn that I can't keep everyone from hurting. I know Dad's an adult. I know he's allowed to make his own choices. It's just weird to realize that the people who took care of you are still figuring things out too."

I thought about Neri, Danse, Iroh, Severus, and everyone who had been old enough to seem certain but human enough to keep learning. I thought about my own first days at Tideglass, when I couldn't remember my name and still had to make decisions about what came next.

"Maybe that's what being alive looks like," I said.

Steven smiled.

"That's a very Dad answer."

"Should I be concerned?"

"Only if you start writing a song."

"I'd be a danger to the music industry."

He laughed. The sound was warm, easier than it had been inside.

I didn't tell him what to think about the Lanternweald or his father's relationships. He hadn't asked me to. We sat until Greg appeared in the doorway holding a dish towel.

"There you are," he said.

"Plotting against you," Steven answered.

"I knew it."

Greg stepped outside and leaned against the railing.

"You're both coming tomorrow?" he asked.

Steven nodded.

"Yeah. I want to see the pier."

The following morning, we went through the Starwake Door together. Greg showed Steven the little stage, the repaired railings, and the spot where the acoustic concert had ended under the lanterns. Steven ran a hand along the sturdy wood, inspected the storage hooks, and asked questions that told me he was paying attention to the practical details rather than expecting magic to solve every problem.

At the far end of the pier, Toph was arguing with Danse about the height of the new handrail.

"That looks right," Steven said.

"It took three meetings to look right," I told him.

"Only three?"

"New record."

Greg laughed.

Then Steven looked back toward Beach City, visible through the doorway.

"I think I understand why you like having two places to go."

"More than two, sometimes," I said.

He nodded.

"And you still have to choose which one you're in."

"Every time."

We spent the morning walking through Lanternwell Square. Iroh offered tea. Mara gave Steven a piece of bread and refused to accept an elaborate thank-you. Maui attempted to impress him by lifting a heavy table and was firmly instructed to put it down because the table had been repaired yesterday.

Steven grinned at that.

By afternoon he was ready to go home.

Greg hugged him beside the door.

"Come back when you want," he said.

"I will."

"Or don't. You can call."

Steven smiled.

"Love you, Dad."

"Love you too, kiddo."

After he left, Greg stood looking at the closed door for a long moment.

"Good visit?" I asked.

"Yeah."

He turned toward me.

"I used to think being a good dad meant having all the answers."

"Did that work?"

"Not even a little."

I slipped my hand into his.

"Maybe it means showing up honestly."

Greg's smile was quiet.

"Steven said something like that."

"He's smart."

"He gets it from me."

"Obviously."

We walked toward the pier, where the late sunlight caught the repaired wood. The doors behind us remained open to anyone who wished to return.

It was enough for today.
